cards.title: C++26 Contracts: Introduction to Preconditions and Postconditions

depth.text: someone can put **function requirements** and **return promises** directly into C++ declarations

A **precondition** says what’s expected on entry; a **postcondition** says what’s expected on normal return. The selected policy can **ignore a check**, report a violation, or stop execution; expected input errors still need ordinary control flow.

cards.camps: Two camps: critics see a fancier runtime assert with questionable value; supporters are bullish on contracts and want to see where they go.

comments.text: I don't like it. I'm all for signing up for a contract if it can turn a runtime error into a compile time error. However, this looks like it just makes more runtime errors. The article also points out a big problem which is "Importantly, this aspect of Contracts is why contract…

This reminds me the "Design by Contract" concept from Eiffel programming language: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_by_contract https://www.eiffel.com/values/design-by-contract/introductio...

cards.title: The Commodore 64 hardware simulator: break chips and pins, see the results

depth.text: someone built a **Commodore 64 simulator** where you can break chips and watch the **board react**

It models the **ASSY 250407 motherboard** pin by pin: lift a chip leg, short it to ground or +5V, remove a chip, or open a resistor, then watch the monitor, keyboard and signals respond. The odd results are **computed from the circuit**, not chosen to match a known fault. It’s for **learning or diagnosis**, not playing games: the simulation runs slower than real time, and a matching symptom is only a clue, not proof.

C64 simulation speed on AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495 (Gorgon Halo)

glossary.hook: A small piece of code that runs automatically when a particular event happens.
glossary.PR: Pull request: a proposed code change shared so others can review it.
glossary.LOC: Lines of code: a count of how many lines a program contains.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.OSS: Open-source software: software whose code is shared so others can inspect it and sometimes reuse it under a license.
glossary.agent: An AI system that can take steps and use tools to get a task done, not just answer questions.
glossary.proof assistant: Software that checks whether a mathematical proof follows its rules.
glossary.kernel: A small program that carries out a calculation on a computer's graphics chip or processor.
glossary.consistent: Here, it means anything the checker accepts can be true in a mathematical world.
glossary.environment: The material Lean has already been given to use while checking a proof.
glossary.model: A mathematical setup where the claims or rules in question all hold.
glossary.set theory: A way of building mathematics from collections of things called sets.
glossary.formal verification: Checking a claim using precise rules, often with a computer.
glossary.Crashpad: A tool apps use to save crash reports for later review.
glossary..dmp file: A file that can hold a snapshot of a program’s memory around a crash.
glossary.sidecar JSON: A companion data file stored alongside another file; here, it goes with a crash dump.
glossary.browser_crashpad_handler: A background helper that manages crash reports for the browser part of an app.
glossary.audio synthesizer: A tool that creates or shapes sounds; this one is for duck audio.
glossary.white noise: A steady, even sound people play to cover other noises or help them relax.
glossary.three.js: A tool for building animated 3D graphics in a web page.
glossary.vibe coding: Making software by telling an AI what you want and letting it write the code, often without closely checking how it works.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: a way for an AI to look up material and use it when answering.
glossary.Markdown: A plain-text way to format notes with headings, lists, and code.
glossary.QPS: Queries per second: how many requests an account can send in one second.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI apps to connect to outside tools.
glossary.SNR: Signal-to-noise ratio: how much useful information there is compared with irrelevant material.
glossary.ESP32: A small computer board that can connect to Wi-Fi and control electronics.
glossary.emulator: A program that imitates another service so you can try your software without using the real one.
glossary.firmware: The built-in software that tells a device's hardware how to work.
glossary.CI: Continuous integration: automatic checks that run when developers change code, helping catch problems early.
glossary.CI/CD: Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery or Deployment: ways to automatically check code changes and get software ready to release.
glossary.IoT: Internet of Things: everyday devices connected to the internet so they can share information or be controlled remotely.
glossary.BLE: Bluetooth Low Energy: a way for nearby devices to exchange data while using little power.
glossary.WebAssembly: A way to run compiled programs inside a web browser.
glossary.flight controller: The part of a drone that controls how it moves.
glossary.framing: The way a film presents someone or something, which can steer how viewers see it.
glossary.villain edit: A way of showing someone so viewers see them as the bad guy.
glossary.ray tracer: A program that makes images by working out how light would bounce around a scene.
glossary.multiple scattering: When light bounces more than once inside something, changing how much light comes back out.
glossary.indirect light: Light that reaches something after bouncing or spreading from elsewhere, rather than coming straight from its source.
glossary.lookup table: A pre-made chart a program checks to find a result instead of working it out each time.
glossary.shader: A small program that tells a game how to draw an image or surface.
glossary.HDR: High Dynamic Range: a way for a screen to show more detail in bright and dark areas.
glossary.tone mapping: A way to fit very bright image values onto a screen so they can be displayed.
glossary.orrery: A model that shows how a planet and its moon move around.
glossary.radiance: A way to describe how much light is traveling in a given direction.
glossary.irradiance: A way to describe how much light arrives on a surface.
glossary.precondition: A condition the caller is expected to have made true before a function starts.
glossary.postcondition: A promise about what will be true if a function finishes normally.
glossary.evaluation semantics: The rule for what happens when a contract check fails.
glossary.contract_assert(...): A check inside a function that says what should be true at that point.
glossary.NDEBUG: A named build setting that makes the usual check disappear when it is defined.
glossary.undefined behavior: A situation where C++ gives no guarantee about what the program will do.
glossary.rate limit: A rule that caps how often someone can make requests to a site.
glossary.automated suspension: A temporary account block triggered by software rather than a person.
glossary.zooxanthellae: Algae that live in coral and help it get energy.
glossary.photosynthesis: The process algae use to turn sunlight into food.
glossary.genet: A group of corals that share the same genetic makeup.
glossary.Adaptive Bleaching Hypothesis: The idea that coral may change the algae it hosts to better suit different conditions.
glossary.horizontal gene transfer: When living things pass genetic instructions between one another outside of having offspring.
glossary.Mermaid: A text-based way to describe a diagram so a tool can draw it.
glossary.SVG: Scalable Vector Graphics: a picture format that stays sharp when resized.
glossary.CSS variables: Named settings in a webpage's styling that you can reuse, such as a color or font.
glossary.FOUC: Flash of Unstyled Content: the brief moment when a page appears before its intended look has loaded.
glossary.subgraph: A smaller group of connected steps inside a diagram.
glossary.reserve asset: Something a country's government keeps as a store of value it can use when needed.
glossary.U.S. Treasury debt: Money the U.S. government has borrowed and still owes.
glossary.central bank: A country's main public bank, which manages money and keeps reserves.
glossary.refinery: A place that cleans up and reshapes gold so it can be sold or used.
glossary.PIT tag: Passive integrated transponder: a tiny tag that helps researchers recognize a fish when it passes a reader.
glossary.diadromous fish: Fish that spend parts of their lives in fresh water and parts in the ocean.
glossary.fishway: A sloping ramp that lets fish get past a dam.
glossary.NOOMBY: Not Out of My Backyard: a label for people who oppose a project near their home.
glossary.source code: The written instructions that tell a computer how to run a program.
glossary.e-voting: Casting votes electronically, rather than using a paper ballot.
glossary.CVR: Cast Vote Record: an electronic record of votes cast in an election.
glossary.RNG: Random number generator: a tool or program that produces numbers meant to seem unpredictable.
glossary.risk limiting audit: A check that uses a sample of paper ballots to catch an election result that may be wrong.
glossary.naturalization: Becoming a citizen of a country where you were not born.
glossary.permanent residency: Permission to live in a country indefinitely, rather than renewing a temporary visa.
glossary.family register: Japan’s official record of a person’s family relationships and key life events.
glossary.Official Gazette: A government publication where official notices are announced.
glossary.Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT: A test of how well someone can use Japanese.
glossary.FTC: Federal Trade Commission: a US agency that investigates businesses and enforces rules meant to protect consumers.
glossary.revocable license: Permission to use a game that a company can take away, rather than something you own.
glossary.offline mode: A way to play a game without connecting to its servers.
glossary.community servers: Servers that players set up and run themselves so they can keep playing together.
glossary.peer-to-peer: A setup where computers talk directly to each other instead of relying on one central server.
glossary.DRM: Digital Rights Management: restrictions in software that control how it can be copied or used.
glossary.Fair Use: A legal rule that allows some uses of copyrighted work without the owner’s permission.
glossary.first sale doctrine: A rule that generally lets someone resell a copy they legally bought.
glossary.copyright: Legal protection that gives creators control over how their work is copied and shared.
glossary.netlist: A map of which electrical connections on a board are joined together.
glossary.oscilloscope: A display that lets you watch an electrical signal change over time.
glossary.PLA: Programmable Logic Array: a chip that helps direct computer requests to the right part.
glossary.FPGA: Field-programmable gate array: a chip that can be set up for different hardware jobs after it is made.
glossary.union-busting: Actions meant to stop workers from forming or joining a union.
glossary.industrial action: When workers act together, often by striking, to push their employer to change something.
glossary.risk score: A number meant to estimate how likely something is to happen.
